posts.content_md:
This is a question about the best way to illuminate photopolymer film.

The beam from my 532nm laser is circular after being expanded. I assume the intensity of the expanded beam is Gaussian.

My film is square. Do I expand the beam so that it is larger than the film area and thus increase the exposure time?

Or is is OK to just fit the circular beam in the center of the film and have the corners underexposed?

I have read that dust and bubbles in the film leave dark spots on the hologram. But I don't know what happens if corners are

left un-illuminated.

Thanks for any input.

Cheers.

posts.content_md:
> **Alan Sailerwrote:↑Mon Oct 07, 2024 2:13 pm:** This is a question about the best way to illuminate photopolymer film.The beam from my 532nm laser is circular after being expanded. I assume the intensity of the expanded beam is Gaussian.

Yes, Gaussian

> **Alan Sailerwrote:↑Mon Oct 07, 2024 2:13 pm:** My film is square. Do I expand the beam so that it is larger than the film area and thus increase the exposure time?Or is is OK to just fit the circular beam in the center of the film and have the corners underexposed?I have read that dust and bubbles in the film leave dark spots on the hologram. But I don't know what happens if corners areleft un-illuminated.Thanks for any input.Cheers.

It's important to illuminate the film as uniformly as possible. The reason is that the material (polymer) reacts to the energy it's "given" by the beam, if the beam is non-uniform, some areas of the film - and so the object - receive more light than other areas, and the polymer "receives" more energy. This may cause some areas of the image to be darker than others, because some areas are over-exposed. It's a common error to see a Single Beam Denisyuk image to be dark, almost black, in the centre because the beam just covered the film area causing over-exposure in the centre due to the Gaussian nature. On the other hand, if you only illuminate the film, and expose as per the beam intensity at the centre, so the corners receive too little light, the corners will be under-exposed, and may be dim. 

As a general rule of thumb, you should expand the beam so that the centre 1/3rd of the beam covers the exposure areas. If your film is 4in x 4in (10cm x 10cm), the centre 1/3rd of the beam should have a diameter of about five and a half inches ( 14 cm) - this is the length of the diagonal. So, the beam should expand to have a diameter of about 12 - 15 in ( 30 - 37cm). This is, as I say, a rule of thumb, but, if you can't expand by this much, you should "overspill" the beam around the film to get it as uniform as possible on the film.

posts.author: Alan Sailer
posts.content_md:
Well amazingly enough my first hologram worked. I am using a basic dennisyuk set-up. I put the hologram plate on top of a three point support and used a first surface mirror to relay the beam up to the plate. That way gravity hold the objects steady. I used the online Geola calculator to set exposure, in this case 90 seconds.

The hologram has the expected problem of dust specs creating black spots. I pretty much knew that was going to happen. But the hologram is bright and well exposed a very pleasing first try. 

Thanks everyone for the help. Now it's time to figure out what is next...

Cheers.

posts.author: Alan Sailer
posts.content_md:
I had a great first result. A few things I learned over the next five exposures

1) the first exposure was 90 seconds with the beam about 12cm diameter visible. The resulting hologram covered about 6 cm.

2) I doubled the distance to the film and got about 10 cm. The exposure was 6 minutes.

3) I asked Geola about the exposure latitude and they said it was nearly impossible to overexpose. So I did a 10 minute exposure.

Almost full coverage. Nice.

It's also nice that I can carefully leave the dark room and not screw up the hologram. I'm not very patient about sitting in a dark room waiting.

I won't make a good holographer....

I now see why people want as much laser power as they can get.

Cheers.
